You are a professional biblical lexicographer fluent in Spanish. Translate the following English lexicon entry into Spanish.

Lemma: H3045

ENGLISH GLOSSES TO TRANSLATE:
  Terse gloss: "to know (cognitively, relationally, carnally); to perceive, understand, recognize, be acquainted with"
  Readable gloss: "A foundational verb spanning cognitive knowledge, personal relationship, and intimate experience. The core Qal sense covers knowing facts and perceiving truth, but the verb extends to relational knowing—being personally acquainted with someone—and even sexual intimacy, where 'he knew her' becomes the Hebrew euphemism for marital union. The causative stems (Hifil, Piel) mean 'to make known' or 'to inform,' while passive forms (Niphal, Pual) express being known or discovered. The reflexive Hitpael captures self-revelation: 'I will make myself known.' This single root weaves together mental perception, personal relationship, and bodily knowledge."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "Qal: to know, perceive, understand"
    Enriched: The overwhelming majority sense: cognitive knowledge spanning facts, situations, and truth. Multilingual glosses converge on 'know' (English), 'conocer/saber' (Spanish), 'connaître/savoir' (French), 'erkennen/wissen' (German), revealing a universal semantic core. Exodus 7:5 ('the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD') exemplifies recognition through divine action.
    Existing Spanish translations: Y-conocerán, Y-sabrá, Y-sabrán, y-sabrán
  Sense 2: "Qal: knower, one who knows (participle as substantive)"
    Enriched: Qal active participle as substantive: 'one who knows,' 'knower,' or even 'acquaintance.' Genesis 3:5 uses this participially ('knowing good and evil'), while Psalm passages speak of 'my acquaintances.' The German 'er weiss' (he knows) and Spanish 'conocedor' (knower) confirm the participial-substantival shift.
    Existing Spanish translations: conoce, conocedor, conocedora-de, conocedores-de, el-que-sabe, que-conoce, que-sabe, que-sepa, quien-supiera, y-conocidos, y-mis-conocidos
  Sense 3: "Hifil: to make known, inform, declare"
    Enriched: Hifil causative: 'to make known,' 'to inform,' 'to teach.' Genesis 41:39 has God making known to Joseph the dream's meaning. The Spanish 'dar a conocer' (to make known) and French 'faire connu' track the causative morphology precisely, showing cross-linguistic alignment in how Hebrew causatives map to Romance periphrastic structures.
    Existing Spanish translations: (conocido), Haz-conocer, dad-a-conocer, e-hizo-conocer, haced-saber, hacednos-saber, hacer-conocer, haciéndote-saber, hazles-saber, hazme-saber, informaste, les-dieron-a-conocer, me-harás-conocer, te-haré-conocer, y-dará-a-conocer, y-harás-conocer, y-haréis-saber
  Sense 4: "Niphal: to be known, become known"
    Enriched: Niphal passive: 'to be known,' 'to become known,' 'to be revealed.' Genesis 41:21 describes how the cows 'could not be known' (no se conocía) to have eaten the fat ones. Exodus 6:3 ('I made myself known') uses the reflexive nuance of Niphal. The passive voice glosses (French 'être connu,' German 'gewusst werden') confirm the passive morphology.
    Existing Spanish translations: Y-será-conocida, fue-descubierto, fui-conocido, me-di-a-conocer, se-conoce, se-conoció, se-da-a-conocer, se-supo, sea-conocida, sea-conocido, será-conocida, será-conocido, y-se-os-hará-saber, y-será-conocida, ¿Acaso-será-conocida
  Sense 5: "Qal: to know carnally (sexual intimacy)"
    Enriched: Sexual intimacy: 'to know carnally.' Genesis 4:1 ('Adam knew Eve his wife') inaugurates this euphemistic use. Spanish 'conoció,' Swahili 'alijua,' and Korean '동침하다' (to sleep with) show how translators navigate this delicate sense—some preserving the euphemism, others opting for clarity.
    Existing Spanish translations: Y-conoció, conocieron, conoció, la-conoció
  Sense 6: "Qal: to know a person, be acquainted with"
    Enriched: Relational, experiential knowledge of persons: to recognize, be acquainted with, have intimate familiarity. Deuteronomy 34:10 speaks of Moses whom 'the LORD knew face to face.' This is not cognitive knowledge about someone, but personal knowing of someone—captured by the direct personal object construction.
    Existing Spanish translations: conocieron, conocieron-lo, conoció, conocían, los-conocieron
  Sense 7: "Qal: infinitive absolute (emphatic surely/certainly)"
    Enriched: Infinitive absolute used adverbially for emphasis: 'surely know,' 'certainly,' 'knowing full well.' 1 Samuel 20:3 has David swearing 'your father surely knows' (saber que sabe). The doubling of the root for intensification is a Semitic idiom reflected in the translations' emphatic phrasing.
    Existing Spanish translations: saber, sabiendo
  Sense 8: ""
    Enriched: Sense unclear from glosses, appearing only in Leviticus 4:23, 28 with specialized cultic vocabulary ('it is made known,' 'fuere dado a conocer'). Likely a passive sense related to sin being revealed or brought to attention.
    Existing Spanish translations: fuere-dado-a-conocer
  Sense 9: "Piel: to cause to know, make to know"
    Enriched: Piel intensive-causative: 'to cause to know,' appearing only in the ketiv/qere textual variants of Job 38:12. The Piel is rarer than Hifil for this semantic function, suggesting intensive or specialized causation.
    Existing Spanish translations: (Q:hiciste-conocer), [K:hiciste-conocer]
  Sense 10: "Hitpael: to make oneself known, reveal oneself"
    Enriched: Hitpael reflexive: 'to make oneself known,' 'to reveal oneself.' Genesis 45:1 has Joseph making himself known to his brothers (Spanish 'darse a conocer'). Numbers 12:6 describes how the LORD makes himself known in visions—active self-disclosure, not passive being-known.
    Existing Spanish translations: al-darse-a-conocer, me-daré-a-conocer
  Sense 11: "Pual: acquaintance, known one (passive participle)"
    Enriched: Pual intensive-passive participle as substantive: 'acquaintance,' 'kinsman,' 'close friend.' Ruth 2:1 introduces Boaz as a 'kinsman' (pariente) of Naomi. The passive participle used nominally indicates someone who is known, i.e., an acquaintance or relative.
    Existing Spanish translations: [pariente], y-conocidos-de-él
  Sense 12: ""
    Enriched: Unclear sense, appearing once in 2 Samuel 19:35 where the elderly Barzillai asks 'Can I discern?' (Spanish 'acaso conozco'). Likely refers to perceptual discernment or ability to distinguish.
    Existing Spanish translations: acaso-conozco
  Sense 13: ""
    Enriched: Unclear sense, appearing once in 1 Samuel 21:3 where David says 'I have directed' (Spanish 'hice saber'). Possibly a causative sense of making known or giving instruction, but the context is ambiguous.
    Existing Spanish translations: hice-saber
